core: Working definition of death: the final stage of the lifespan, the endpoint of development from conception until death ('womb to tomb')
Biological working definition of death: the physical event in which the body's systems stop working (absence of breathing and heartbeat)
The dying process: dying trajectories (sudden death, terminal illness, organ failure, frailty) and terminal decline as a gradual, progressive loss of function
The Kübler-Ross model: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance — attributed to Elisabeth Kübler-Ross (1969), presented as a model, not a law
Grief and bereavement: grief as a normal response to loss, with mental and physical reactions (MedlinePlus, NCI)
Death across cultures: mourning and burial/funeral practices differ across cultures and individuals
Honest note: 'dying well' is a modern idea with many meanings; no universal agreement on a good death
Honest framing: death gives life its shape; the ending frames every earlier stage
supporting: Grief vs. mourning vs. bereavement as distinct concepts (internal feeling, outward expression, period after a death)
How long bereavement lasts depends on closeness, whether the death was expected, and other factors
Normal grief begins soon after a loss and fades over time; mental health professionals generally do not regard grief as something to be 'fixed'
Other theories of grief exist alongside Kübler-Ross's (narrative models, dual-process model), supporting the model-not-law framing
outOfScope: Aging and late adulthood as developmental stages (own sibling topic: aging; cognitive-aging; social-aging)
End-of-life care practice: hospice, palliative care procedures, care decisions, advance directives (owned by the nursing subject)
Death ethics: euthanasia, medical aid in dying, moral arguments about the ethics of death and dying (owned by the philosophy subject)
Bereavement treatment, complicated-grief diagnosis, or clinical advice
Statistics on causes of death, mortality rates, or life-expectancy data

claims.claim: Lifespan development is the scientific study of human growth and change from conception until death, so death is the final stage of the lifespan — the endpoint of the human developmental course.

Death is a physical event in which the body's systems stop working, including the absence of breathing and a heartbeat; it also has psychological dimensions (how people cope, prepare, and grieve) and social dimensions (how dying people are treated and how culture shapes beliefs about death).

The dying process follows different trajectories: sudden death (abrupt loss of function, as in heart attack, stroke, accidents), terminal illness (gradual loss of function, as in many cancers), organ failure (overall gradual decline with cycles of improvement and setback), and frailty (steady gradual decline without cycles of improvement). Terminal decline is the slow, progressive loss of function in the final phase of a fatal illness.

Elisabeth Kübler-Ross, a Swiss psychiatrist, described five responses people commonly show as they face their own death — denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance — based on interviews with terminally ill patients and set forth in On Death and Dying (1969).

The five Kübler-Ross responses are a model, not a law: researchers describe them as themes rather than fixed stages, people experience them in their own order (skipping or revisiting responses), grief varies across individuals and cultures, the model is debated, and other theories of grief exist.

Grief is a normal response to loss: grief is the internal emotional reaction to a loss, mourning is its outward public expression, and bereavement is the period after the death of a loved one; normal grief begins soon after a loss and fades over time, and mental health professionals generally do not regard grief as something that needs to be 'fixed'.

Grief can be a mental, physical, social, or emotional reaction: mental reactions can include anger, guilt, anxiety, sadness, and despair; physical reactions can include sleeping problems and changes in appetite; how long bereavement lasts depends on how close the survivor was to the person who died, whether the death was expected, and other factors.

A person's grief is shaped by personality, age, sex, cultural and religious background, coping skills, social support, and the relationship with the person who died; the way people mourn is affected by beliefs, religious practices, and culture, and burial and funeral practices differ across cultures.

'Dying well' is a modern idea with many meanings: the modern Western notion of a good death — peaceful, dignified, pain-free, at home, with enough time to prepare — is one description, but there is no universal agreement about what makes a good death, which varies with culture, religion, family, and history.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Status of the Kübler-Ross five responses: popularly treated as fixed 'stages' everyone passes through in order, while the underlying research literature treats them as themes that vary by person, order, and culture.
positions: Popular usage (and many summaries) present denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance as a fixed five-stage sequence.
OpenStax (following Kübler-Ross's own framing) describes them as 'themes' rather than stages — emotional and behavioral priorities, not milestones to reach.

OpenStax notes grief patterns vary across individuals, cultures, and context, and presents other theories of grief (narrative models, the dual-process model) alongside Kübler-Ross's, which is 'perhaps the best-known theory of grief, but not the only one.'
NCI PDQ: grief is affected by personality, age, cultural and religious background, and social support; mourning is affected by beliefs, religious practices, and culture.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the Kübler-Ross responses as a model, not a law: the five are named and attributed to Kübler-Ross (1969), then framed as themes people may experience in any order, with the explicit honest note that grief is individual and the model is debated. No claim of a fixed universal sequence is made.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How grief is classified: 'normal' grief vs. 'complicated' grief, and whether grief is something to treat or something to let run its course.
positions: MedlinePlus and NCI: grief and mourning are part of the normal process of dealing with a loss; normal grief begins soon after a loss and symptoms go away over time.
NCI distinguishes anticipatory, normal/common, and complicated grief, where complicated grief lasts longer than normal grief.
OpenStax: mental health professionals generally do not regard grief as something that needs to be 'fixed.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson stays strictly within the normal-grief claims (mental and physical reactions, variation in duration) and does not diagnose, classify, or advise on complicated grief or treatment, which are out of scope.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's claims that death and dying is 'a foundational concept in Human Development' and that its value is mainly 'organizing information' for college assignments — boilerplate with no attributable facts.
The draft's vocabulary entry defining 'Death And Dying' circularly as 'A foundational Human Development concept covered in this lesson.'
The draft's framing of the lesson as teaching 'how to reason with the concept' rather than describing what death and dying actually are in developmental terms.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced generic boilerplate with a source-verified working definition: death as the final stage of the lifespan, the endpoint of development from conception until death (OpenStax 1.1, 17.1).
Added the dying process with the four dying trajectories (sudden death, terminal illness, organ failure, frailty) and terminal decline, attributed to OpenStax 17.1, with original examples.

Added the Kübler-Ross model (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) attributed to Kübler-Ross's 1969 On Death and Dying, explicitly framed as a model, not a law, with the honest note that grief is individual and the model is debated (OpenStax 17.3, Britannica).
Added grief/bereavement as a normal process with mental and physical reactions (MedlinePlus, NCI), distinguishing grief, mourning, and bereavement.
Added the one-line cultural note that mourning and burial/funeral practices differ across cultures (OpenStax 17.1, NCI).
Added the honest note that 'dying well' is a modern idea with many meanings (OpenStax 17.4).
Added the honest framing that death gives life its shape.
Kept end-of-life care practice and death ethics out of scope (nursing and philosophy subjects own those).

Supports the framing of lifespan development as the scientific study of growth, change, and stability in humans from conception until death ('womb to tomb'), which grounds the working definition of death as the final stage of the lifespan. Reference only; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: 17.1 Biological, Psychological, and Social Aspects of Death and Dying — Lifespan Development 2e
sourceRecords.notes: New id minted (no existing registry record). Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: death as a physical event in which the body's systems stop working (absence of breathing and heartbeat); clinical vs. biological death; the psychological and social dimensions of death; the four dying trajectories (sudden death, terminal illness, organ failure, frailty); cultural variation in burial and funeral practices (e.g., Apache, Navajo, Nigerian examples). Used for the working definition, the dying-process section, and the culture note. Reference only; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: 17.3 Coping with Death — Lifespan Development 2e
sourceRecords.notes: New id minted (no existing registry record). Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: grief as the internal emotional reaction to loss, mourning as its outward behavioral manifestation, bereavement as the experience of the death of a loved one; Kübler-Ross's five themes (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) from interviews with hospice patients, with the explicit point that 'themes' is more appropriate than 'stages'; no one right way to respond to death; grief as a normal, understandable reaction; variation across individuals and cultures; other theories of grief. Central source for the Kübler-Ross section and the model-not-law framing. Reference only; no wording reproduced.
